# ferrotherm

> Thermodynamic computing in pure Rust: sparse energy-based models, chromatic block-Gibbs,
> parallel tempering, thermodynamic linear algebra, stochastic differentiable programs, a
> variational compiler onto device graph topologies, and a joules ledger pricing every operation
> against swappable device models. Zero dependencies, std-only, wasm-clean, deterministic by seed.
> Every module is verified against exact physics (Onsager 1944, exhaustive ground states,
> Gaussian elimination, finite-difference gradients) in `cargo test`.

Install: `cargo add ferrotherm` (or git: https://github.com/dcharlot-physicalai-bmi/ferrotherm)

## Docs

- [README](https://github.com/dcharlot-physicalai-bmi/ferrotherm/blob/main/README.md): layer map, verification results, measured numbers with provenance labels
- [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/dcharlot-physicalai-bmi/ferrotherm/blob/main/AGENTS.md): invariants, task recipes, contribution rules for AI agents
- [API docs](https://docs.rs/ferrotherm): module-level docs carry the math and its sources

## Start here if you are solving a problem, not studying a sampler

`model` is the layer most callers want. State a problem as variables with domains, constraints that
must hold, and an objective; it compiles to spins and answers in your own names. Everything below it
works in couplings and biases, which is the machine's language rather than the problem's.

Values are the modeller's own values everywhere, never slot indices: an integer over 10..=20 takes
the value 13, and 3 is an error naming the range. `feasible` means every variable decoded AND every
constraint held; when it is false, `violated` names what was broken and `did_not_decode` names the
variables whose encoding lost. A penalty makes a constraint expensive, not impossible.

Reachable from Rust, C (include/ferrotherm.h), Python (python/ferrotherm), Zig (zig/ferrotherm.zig),
Julia (julia/Ferrotherm), wasm, the node editor, an HTTP API and an MCP server. Every one of them
compiles through the same code, so an answer does not depend on which door you came in.

## Key modules

- model: variables, constraints (not_equal, equal, fix, cardinality, at_most, at_least, exactly-one,
  at-most-one), linear and quadratic objectives; compiles to spins, decodes by name, checks itself
- encode: one-hot, binary and domain-wall encodings of a categorical variable
- certify: what a run ACTUALLY did, computed from its samples -- effective beta, ESS, integrated
  autocorrelation time, TV from the exact distribution beside the sampling noise floor
- ftp: the portable program format every backend reads (spec/ftp-v1.md is normative)
- exact, planted, oracle: answers known before the machine is asked -- variable elimination, planted
  ground states, and a solver trait including one that exists to fail
- fabric, conform: what a device can do, and a conformance suite that can reject a machine
- graph, gibbs: sparse pairwise EBMs, chromatic block-Gibbs with clamping
- device: published degree-16 grid topology of Z1-class thermodynamic chips
- ledger: joules accounting (samples/reads/writes x device Prices; Z1_SPICE = vendor pre-silicon estimates)
- tempering: simulated annealing + parallel tempering (replica exchange), ladder-health diagnostics
- tla: thermodynamic linear algebra (OU network solves SPD systems, samples N(A^-1 b, A^-1/beta))
- program: stochastic differentiable circuits; REINFORCE + parameter-shift + FD-referee gradients
- compile: variational compilation of conditionals onto device patches; chain-rule KL error bound
- ffi: C ABI (ft_*) for wasm and host languages, including the whole modelling layer (ft_model_*)
  and the native higher-order path (ft_hubo_*)
- hubo: higher-order models solved WITHOUT quadratising -- no ancillas, no penalty to get right

## Examples (each is a verification gate, exit code = pass/fail)

- ring_tv, onsager: sampler vs exact Boltzmann / Onsager closed form
- z1_ledger: generative vs 100 Hz control regimes priced at vendor SPICE costs
- grad_check, gibbs_grad, lqr_energy: gradient cross-validation; trained controller vs provable optimum
- compile_chain, reach_on_z1: compilation error bound verified exactly; the control-workload boundary
- flips_bench: CPU throughput anchor

## Servers, for an agent

- `ferrotherm-serve`: an HTTP API and an MCP server over the same operations. Ten MCP tools
  (sample, anneal, energy, verify, bound, exact_planar, toroidal_bound, optimize, solve,
  capabilities); reach for `ferrotherm_solve` first, since every other tool wants a graph of spins
  and returns an array of +/-1. `/v1/capabilities` describes the HTTP side, by GET or POST.
- The node editor exposes `window.ferrotherm` for scripted use: `ready`, `types()`, `add`, `set`,
  `connect`, `find`, `run()`, `toJson`/`fromJson`, `check()`. See web-tests/editor.test.mjs, which
  drives exactly that surface.

## The model you write and the picture a person edits are the same document

`window.ferrotherm.fromModel(m)` lays out the SAME JSON `ferrotherm_solve` takes -- variables,
constraints, objective -- as a node graph, and `toModel()` reads it back. So a model you write can
be opened, moved, extended by hand and returned to you without going through a second notation, and
you never have to author node positions: they are computed, because the model has none.

Two gates hold that claim up rather than asserting it. `scripts/check-editor-parity.sh` says every
Constraint variant in the model layer is reachable from a node -- it exists because the layer had
nine and the editor offered six for as long as nothing compared the lists. `scripts/check-editor-model.sh`
puts one model through both doors and compares the COMPILED size, because an editor that silently
drops a `k` still draws, still runs, and answers a different question. Both refuse to be believed
without a `--selftest` that damages the thing under test and demands a failure.

What has no drawing is refused rather than approximated: a counting constraint whose literals name
DIFFERENT values has no node (a counting node holds one value for all of them), and `fromModel`
says so instead of drawing the one it can. That model still runs through HTTP and MCP.

## Higher-order terms: two paths, and they are not equivalent

A term over three or more variables can go two ways, and both are reachable from every surface.

- **Quadratised.** `objective` with `of: [...]` (or `ft_model_objective_product`) lowers it through
  Rosenberg's reduction: one ancilla per substituted pair, plus a penalty. The reply reports
  `ancillas`, and the guarantee is about finding OPTIMA rather than about sampling.
- **Native.** `hubo` / `ft_hubo_*` / `Hubo` (Python, Zig, Julia) solves it as written. A term of any
  width contributes `-w * prod(s_i)`; no ancillas exist to get right.

The difference is measured, not argued. `examples/hubo_vs_reduction` gives the reduced arm its best
beta ladder and up to 1024x the budget: on 60 three-body terms over 40 spins the native path reaches
-48.12 and the reduced path reaches -34.00 at a thousand times the work. The mechanism is the
penalty, chosen as the sum of every coefficient's magnitude and therefore ~1300 against term weights
of 1 -- any flip that would move the search must first pay it, so the landscape is rigid rather than
merely larger. Zero ancilla violations across 384 runs confirms it: stuck inside the feasible region,
not wandering out of it.

So: reach for `hubo` when the model IS higher-order and the target is a CPU. Reach for the
quadratised path when the target is pairwise hardware, which is what the reduction is for.
`scripts/check-hubo-answers.sh` puts a three-body parity term -- the smallest model that cannot be
expressed pairwise at all -- through Rust, Python, Zig and Julia and compares the energy, the state
invariant, and the ancilla count, so a surface that quietly reduced it is caught reporting the wrong
saving for the right answer.

`ancillas_avoided` is an UPPER BOUND, not a cost: the reduction shares one ancilla across every term
containing the same pair, so on three terms sharing one it spends one where the count reports three.

## Constraints, all nine of them

not_equal, equal, fix, cardinality (exactly k), at_most, at_least, exactly_one, at_most_one,
all_different. Reach for `all_different` for assignment, scheduling, colouring and puzzles: it
lowers per shared value rather than per pair, so it needs no slack and costs nothing where two
domains do not overlap. Prefer exactly_one / at_most_one over k = 1 -- at_most with k = 1 buys a
slack variable it does not need, and the compiler says so in `caveats`.

ANY constraint takes `soft: w`, which makes it a PREFERENCE priced at w rather than a rule. The
solver may trade it away, the answer stays feasible, and the reply reports it under `violated` with
`"hard": false` plus a `cost`. Hard for what an answer must satisfy to be an answer; soft for what
you would like.

Encodings: one-hot (default, exact), domain-wall (exact, one spin fewer per variable IN ISOLATION
-- across a pairwise constraint the lowering pays ancillas and it loses, measured 9 spins against
one-hot's 8), binary (fewest spins, but REFUSED in any constraint or objective, since a binary
indicator is a product of every bit). The node editor offers the first two for that reason.
